title: Journey to the Overland - Part 1 - Introduction
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxwGfKCo6as

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens a series on Dino Seaware's *Journey to the Overland*, and the best description he can find is that it plays like someone's decades-long house-ruled hack of a game, finally codified. It began as a childhood world of make-believe and grew from there.

The scale is the headline. First edition ran 170 pages; the second runs close to 600. It is a solo open-world hex crawl in which you create a character, start in a town, and roam — sailing, joining guilds, learning skills, building roads, buying property, paying taxes, marrying, working jobs. Five long objectives frame it: gather the five weapons of power, raise gold for an army, recruit allies, overthrow the king, and defeat the warden Morkai. Turns run on a calendar, with a weekly event card and a daily weather card that gates travel.

Crucially it isn't a book to read cover to cover. You read the opening section, start playing, and look things up — though Daniel found real gaps where terms appear in neither index nor contents.

He's frank about the flavour: the lore draws heavily on Christian mythology, the art is often printed at poor resolution, and one rule states a man may only marry a woman — which he flags plainly. The influence he names is *Barbarian Prince*.

----

A 600-page solo RPG you're meant to learn by stumbling through it rather than reading first. Does that approach appeal, or exhaust you?
